questions.q: What is the capstone project in this chapter?
options: A command-line tool, ask.py, that takes a prompt as a CLI argument, calls a real API, and prints the formatted response
A web application with a graphical user interface
A database schema design exercise
A multiple-choice exam covering the whole course
questions.explain: The capstone is a CLI tool: it reads a prompt from the command line, sends it to an API, and prints the result, with proper error handling, tests, and type hints.

questions.q: Why must the prompt be accepted as a command-line argument rather than hard-coded into the script?
options: Hard-coding is actually required by the "done" checklist
Python cannot read command-line arguments
It has no real benefit — either approach is equally acceptable
A hard-coded prompt would make the tool useless for anyone who wants to ask something different without editing the source code
questions.explain: The whole point of a CLI tool is flexibility — a user should be able to run it with any prompt they want without touching the code. Hard-coding the prompt would defeat that purpose, which is why it's explicitly part of the "done" checklist.

questions.q: According to the lesson's "done" checklist, what must the error handling in ask.py cover?
options: Only successful responses — errors are out of scope
Only network timeouts
A missing API key, a timeout, and a bad response, without crashing with a raw traceback
Nothing — error handling is optional for this project
questions.explain: The checklist specifically calls for handling a missing API key, a timeout, and a bad response gracefully — the tool should fail with a clear message, not an unhandled traceback dumped to the user.

questions.q: Which chapter's skills does the lesson say the capstone's client-wrapper design is modeled on?
options: Chapter 2's dictionaries lesson
Chapter 3's class-based client wrapper lesson (Lesson 17)
Chapter 6's async lessons
Chapter 4's dependency conflicts lesson
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly points back to Chapter 3, Lesson 17 — writing a simple class-based client wrapper — as the pattern the capstone's API client class follows.

questions.q: Besides a working API call, what two Chapter 7 skills does the "done" checklist require in the capstone?
options: At least two pytest tests and type hints on the main functions
A GUI and a database connection
Async/await and a Docker container
A linter configuration file and nothing else
questions.explain: The checklist specifically requires at least two pytest tests covering parts that don't need a live network call, plus type hints on the main functions — both drawn directly from Chapter 7, Testing & Code Quality.
